residents.research_note: THE OLDEST LIVING RESIDENT, AND THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THE PARCEL WHOSE ARRIVAL DATE THIS PROJECT HAD TO REFUSE TO GUESS - UNTIL A SENTENCE TURNED UP. Everything about Hubbard's later Chicago life was documented here and the date he first came was a fact everyone knew and nothing in data/sources/ stated, so it was carried as a conjecture citing nothing and left visibly empty rather than quietly filled: it was the case AGENTS.md rule 1 exists for. Hurlbut's American Fur Company chapter, read for T-0575 and cited by this record since T-0594, closes it - Montreal 13 May 1818, Mackinaw 4 July, Chicago the last day of October or the first of November - and the asymmetry that was worth leaving visible is now a smaller and more interesting one. The sentence is the COMPILER'S, not the man's: it stands outside the quotation marks in which Hubbard speaks four lines later, so a date this project had no source for at all now has a source of 1881 at rung 4, and the record says both things on its face rather than letting the citation look like an attestation. The inverse must be legal; the mirror row must exist. A row with no far end is not a weaker kin row, it is one with the entire checked part removed, and a graded name with nothing checking it is a note. The second reading would also have made every genealogical name in the corpus eligible for a residents layer that reconstructs a town on one day. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Peter Pruyne,” (f1839_v0036, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Pruyne' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins P. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 7 times, as “PRUYNE P”, “PRUYNE PETER”, 1833-10-24 to 1836-06-24: 2 federal land entries — E2SW sec 30 T39N R13E; W2NW sec 30 T39N R13E and 2 lots in the platted town — lot 2 of block 58 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL58CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 17 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3B17CHIOT, as printed) and 3 parcels of the school section — lot 1 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 3 of block 119 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 8 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 167.83 acres stated in all, for $17153.79 (ls0321, ls0323, ls0324, ls0858, ls0859, ls1436, ls1437). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $16750.00 to the money. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_letter_list names this person at Chicago by 1 April 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Smith, William V.” (poll_1835_072, line 359). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. citations.citation: The baptismal register of St Mary's, Chicago — the first Catholic parish in the town — opened by Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr on 22 May 1833 and read here for the years 1833, 1834 and 1835: 57 entries in French and English naming children, parents, godparents and witnesses, with the priest's own signature under every one and eight autographs of the town's own people beside them.

transcribes.work: The baptismal register kept at Chicago by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from May 1833
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and these eleven images are photographs of it. A reading made off them is scan_verified — the higher of this project's two reading grades — and it outranks the marriage and death pages of st_cyr_register_ichr_v4, which reached this project through a 1921-22 article and a web transcription.

what_it_supplies: 57 dated baptisms of 1833-1835 and 267 named readings of people — 46 of the entries at Chicago and 166 of the readings adults there
KINSHIP, which no other source this project holds gives at all: a child, its two parents and its two godparents on one dated line, 44 times over
the town's Catholic population — French, Métis, Irish and German — of whom 85 distinct adults reach no surname in the residents layer

eight AUTOGRAPHS: Mark Beaubien, Josette Laframboise, Augustin Bonné, Monique Nadeau, Jean Baptiste Lavigne, J. B. Beaubien, Robert A. Kinzie and Gwinthlean Whistler signing under the priest, each placing a named person at a named place on a named day in their own hand
two adult baptisms with AGES — Josette Laframboise Beaubien at 38 in June 1834 and Geneviève Medera at about 20 in June 1835 — which are the only ages this project has for either woman
the parish's own start date, 22 May 1833, on a page the book heads '1er Page'
the register's own arithmetic: pencil tallies of 19, 24 and 14 baptisms for 1833, 1834 and 1835, which check any reading of it
a hue and cry on the title page describing what a young man of the Illinois country wore in 1833 or 1834 — a white pea coat, gray pants and a fur cap
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, street, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town, and names no church building on any of the eleven pages
residence, and this is the trap. A baptism documents a person at a font on a day. Presence is not residence and nothing here mints or regrades a resident
presence on 1 July 1835 for anyone not baptised or standing as sponsor within days of it
occupation. One entry writes 'Doctor Egan' — a title inside a name — and that is the only trade the book ever states

ALL CHICAGO. Entries 1-11 of 1834 were written at Bear Creek, the South Fork of the Sangamon and Springfield, in Sangamon County, on the priest's journey back from St. Louis. A reader who takes the book as a Chicago roll plants eleven households in the wrong county
reliable spelling. A French priest wrote Irish, English and German names and phoneticised Potawatomi and Odawa ones; the same woman is Nadeau, Nodeau and Nodou in his own hand on three pages
the sponsors of 1834 entry 4, which stood on a line the scan's frame cuts off
anything about 1836 or later. The two page-sides in the deposit that carry 1837-38 and 1849 entries are declared and not transcribed
